# Exodus 1: Research notes, verse by verse

**Gaps:** I couldn't find anything on this chapter from bibleodyssey.org, oca.org (Orthodox), or the Pentecostal, Lutheran-specific or Anglican sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those are left out. The main page for verses 12–14 was cut off, so those notes are thin. Only one verse divides teachers in a real way: whether the midwives lied in v. 19. That split runs more between Catholic moral theology and Protestant commentators than between Protestant denominations.

---

**v. 1:** The Hebrew opens with "And." The Pulpit Commentary says this links Exodus directly to Genesis, as if each writer were continuing one book. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Pulpit stresses "every man and his household." It argues each family brought servants and dependants, which helps explain how Israel later grew so large. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Guzik: Exodus picks up where Genesis ends, with a large family that has a crucial place in God's plan. The first verses of Exodus reach back some 430 years. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Exd/Exd-1.cfm

**vv. 2–4:** Pulpit: the sons of Leah and Rachel come first, oldest to youngest, then the sons of the secondary wives. It thinks this order honours lawful marriage over secondary unions. Joseph is left off because he didn't "come into Egypt with Jacob." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm

**v. 5:** Ellicott counts the seventy this way: Jacob himself, 1; his sons, 12; his daughter, Dinah, 1; his grandsons, 51; his grand-daughter Serah, 1; his great-grandsons, 4--Total, 70. https://biblehub.com/exodus/1-5.htm
- Pulpit: counting Jacob among his own descendants is a normal Hebrew way of speaking, and objecting to it is nitpicking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Gill: the small number is given so readers can compare it with the multitude who later left Egypt (Exod 12:37). https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/exodus/1-5.html
- **Seventy or seventy-five?** The Greek Septuagint reads seventy-five. Barnes: It is evident that Stephen has followed the account which is given by the Septuagint in Acts 7:14. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/acts/7-14.html. Cambridge lists the five extra names: grandsons and a great-grandson of Joseph through Manasseh and Ephraim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/7-14.htm. Precept Austin notes that one Hebrew manuscript from Qumran also has 75. It concludes regardless of which figure is used (seventy or seventy-five), the number is actual, not figurative. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-1-commentary
- *Modern scholarship:* the Cambridge Bible reads the number through source criticism. It thinks the "P" writer meant seventy *not counting* Jacob, while others counted him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/1.htm

**v. 6:** Pulpit: "all that generation" means the sons' wives, Dinah, and the grown members of their households. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm. Guzik: eventually, Joseph died and the status his family enjoyed died with him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Exd/Exd-1.cfm

**v. 7:** Pulpit: the writer piles up four near-synonym verbs and a doubled "very, very" to show astonishing growth, a family becoming a nation. It defends a two-million population by assuming 430 years and large households, and notes that scholars split between 430 and 215 years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Cambridge: Hebrew tradition loved to tell of the wonderful increase of their ancestors in Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/1.htm

**v. 8:** Pulpit thinks "new king" probably, though not certainly, means a new dynasty with new policies. It suggests Rameses I or Seti I, partly because of the city name "Rameses" in v. 11. "Did not know Joseph" means he knew nothing of Joseph's history. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Cambridge: the phrase implies the rise of a king whose reign began a new policy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/1.htm
- Bible Hub study notes: the new ruler chose not to honour Joseph's memory, but God does not forget His servants or His promises. https://biblehub.com/exodus/1-8.htm

**v. 9:** Pulpit: "more and mightier than we" may not mean Israel actually outnumbered Egypt. It is the kind of exaggeration rulers use to justify extreme measures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm

**v. 10:** Pulpit cites ancient examples of rulers using crushing labour to keep a people down. It links the fear of war to threats from the Hittites, and notes Pharaoh also feared losing a productive workforce if Israel left. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm

**v. 11:** Pulpit: "taskmasters" literally means "lords of tribute," an Egyptian title for overseers of forced labour. "Store cities" held supplies and weapons. It places Pithom near Bubastis and links Rameses with the city Rameses II favoured. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm
- Cambridge reports Naville's excavations, where inscriptions showed a site's ancient name was P-etôm, "Abode of Etôm." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/exodus/1.htm

**v. 12:** Pulpit: "grieved" is too weak. The Hebrew verb The more they are oppressed by a new king, the more they multiply. (Bible Hub outline) and conveys "a mixture of loathing and alarm." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/1.htm. The NET translation reads "the Egyptians loathed the Israelites." https://bible.org/seriespage/11-exodus-1-%E2%80%93-4-egyptian-captivity-and-moses-called

**vv. 13–14:** The only commentary I found here was a Bible Hub cross-reference page. It calls the move from forced labour (vv. 11–14) to secret infanticide (v. 16) a crafty shift from brute force (Exodus 1:11-14) to covert infanticide. https://biblehub.com/exodus/1-15.htm

**v. 15:** *Were the midwives Hebrews or Egyptians?* The Hebrew allows either.
- Ellicott: the names Shiphrah ("beautiful") and Puah ("one who cries out") are Semitic. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
- Benson and Barnes think they were Egyptians. Poole, Gill and Keil & Delitzsch say Hebrews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
- Most (Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Gill, Clarke) take the two women as heads of a guild, expected to pass orders to the rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm. Guzik agrees: probably the "presidents" of an "association of midwives." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Exd/Exd_1.cfm
- Gill reports a Jewish tradition (the Targums) that they were Jochebed and Miriam. He rejects it for Miriam, who was only a girl. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
- *Modern scholarship:* Cambridge says a people anywhere near 600,000 men would need far more than two midwives. So either the numbers were in reality very much less, or these were the only midwives whose names were remembered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
- Bible Hub study note: the text names the two women but leaves Pharaoh unnamed. https://biblehub.com/exodus/1-15.htm

**v. 16:** Keil & Delitzsch: the Hebrew for "birthstool" is the same word used for a potter's wheel in Jeremiah 18:3. The midwives were to watch the birth closely and kill boys as they were born. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
- Pulpit: infanticide was a crime in Egypt, but a god-king's order could make almost anything legitimate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm

**v. 17:** Guzik: The civil government commanded something that was clearly against God's command. The midwives did the only right thing: they obeyed God rather than man. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Exd/Exd_1.cfm
- *Reformed (Calvin):* the midwives' example is enough to condemn those who excuse obeying wicked orders, especially since the Holy Spirit himself commends them, as not having obeyed the king, because they feared God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-17.html
- Constable: because their fear of God gave them reverence for life, the midwives refused to kill. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-19.html

**v. 18:** Bible.org: Pharaoh summoned them to court to explain their disobedience. They knew they risked punishment and stayed committed to God anyway. https://blogs.bible.org/taking-a-stand-for-what-is-right/

**v. 19: The main dispute. Did the midwives lie?**
- *Lied, but were not rewarded for lying:* Pulpit plainly says they made an untrue excuse. https://biblehub.com/exodus/1-15.htm. Coffman: their testimony was false because it aimed to deceive, though it contained real facts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-19.html. Constable notes the Bible doesn't stop to condemn the lie here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-15.html
- *Perhaps no lie at all:* Guzik suggests the Hebrew women may really have been hardier, and the midwives simply didn't give every reason. He quotes a commentator (cited in the style of Gill) who says there was nothing but truth, though they did not speak the whole truth, which they were not obliged to do. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Exd/Exd_1.cfm. A Pulpit homily says the midwives may simply have stayed away so the women delivered on their own. https://biblehub.com/sermons/exodus/1-15.htm
- *Evangelical middle view (GotQuestions):* it seems a lie, possibly a half-truth. God is never said to commend the lie, and they were rewarded not for their words but for their works. https://www.gotquestions.org/Hebrew-midwives.html
- *Wider debate:* Bible.org: it is unclear whether they told the truth, and the question has long been a matter of debate within biblical ethics. https://blogs.bible.org/taking-a-stand-for-what-is-right/
- *Catholic, Augustine:* God rewarded not because they lied, but because they were merciful to God's people. He forgave the evil for the sake of the good. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1313.htm. Augustine argues truly holy women would have refused both the lie and the killing. https://biblehub.com/library/augustine/against_lying/section_34_but_some_man.htm. Elsewhere he says the approval reflects their progress toward better things, since lying out of mercy to save a life is a step toward that. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1312.htm
- *Catholic, Aquinas:* they were rewarded for fearing God and for their good will, But the subsequent lie was not meritorious. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/summa.SS_Q110_A3.html. He cites Gregory the Great's view that because of the lie, their reward shrank from an eternal one to an earthly one. He also cites Jerome's view that God built them "spiritual houses." https://ccel.org/ccel/aquinas/summa.SS_Q110_A4.html
- *Catholic, modern apologetics (catholic.com):* it was not a lie but a *mental reservation*. Their general statement about Hebrew women was true, and Pharaoh wrongly took it as a report of what they themselves had seen. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/blog/no-god-did-not-bless-a-lie

**v. 20:** GotQuestions: Israel kept growing, and the text gives the reason for God's blessing as the midwives' fear of God, not their words. https://www.gotquestions.org/Hebrew-midwives.html. Coffman: God rewarded them for fearing him and helping his purpose of multiplying Israel, not for deceiving Pharaoh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-19.html. Pulpit: Pharaoh's second plan failed like the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm

**v. 21:** Bible.org suggests the midwives may not have had children before. God honoured their faith by giving them families. https://blogs.bible.org/taking-a-stand-for-what-is-right/
- A Pulpit homily: kindness shown to God's people never fails of its reward. https://biblehub.com/sermons/exodus/1-15.htm. Matthew Henry: services done for God's Israel are often repaid in kind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm

**v. 22:** Calvin: when his tricks failed, the tyrant now shakes off fear and flies to open violence. He gave the job to all Egyptians so there would be no lack of executioners. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-22.html
- Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist): the Nile was sacred, so Pharaoh may have meant the babies as an offering to his god. Constable similarly suggests obeying the order became an act of worship. He thinks the plan failed because ordinary Egyptians don't seem to have cooperated. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-22.html
- Gill: "every son" means Hebrew sons only, as the Targums and Septuagint make clear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-22.html. Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran) also call this open violence after the second plan failed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/1-22.html
- Ellicott shows that infanticide was common in the ancient world (Sparta, Athens, Rome), so the order is not unlikely. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-22.htm
- NET note: the order about girls may be a permission rather than a command. The verse is the chapter's climax and leads into Moses being saved by Pharaoh's own daughter. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Exo&chapter=1&lang=de&tab=commentaries&verse=22
- Ways of reading it as part of the Bible's larger story: Bible Hub links it to Genesis 3:15 (the serpent's offspring against the woman's) and to Herod's massacre (Matt 2:16). https://biblehub.com/q/What_does_Exodus_1_22_mean.htm. It also notes the irony that the river of death becomes Moses' cradle of rescue. https://biblehub.com/study/exodus/1-22.htm. Matthew Henry calls it the enmity of the seed of the serpent, against the Seed of the woman. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/1-15.htm
